props.title: Badge
props.description: A short label that names a state or a count. It is not interactive, so it wears only the resting state of a control recipe and deliberately skips the shared state machine — a label that changed colour under the pointer would read as something you can press. Pick the recipe with `variant`, pick the ramp it resolves against with `tint`.

props.title: Variant and tint
props.description: Every combination the two axes allow — three of the six recipes, the ones that read as a label rather than as a control — plus the one variant the badge owns. `raised` is paper fill and quiet ink, no ramp: the chip that sits on a grey card, where a `tinted` neutral would sink into the card and a `filled` one would shout. There is no `normal` or `plain` badge, because both would be text with padding around it.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Each size borrows the padding of the control size one step below it, and sets its label in the caption face, so a badge reads as a label rather than as a control that stopped working.

props.title: Where it lands
props.description: The trailing cell of a table, the trailing slot of a preference row, the count on a navigation row. In all three it annotates something the row already names, which is why it stays small and never carries the only copy that matters. A leading dot needs no prop: the badge is an inline flex row and the glyph inherits its content colour.

props.title: Button
props.description: The six control recipes, each on any ramp. Hover, press, and disabled are not written here at all — `data-control` puts the recipe's own states on the element, so a button's stylesheet is the box and nothing else.

props.title: Variants
props.description: `normal` is the neutral control on the paper, edged by a hairline; `recessed` is the same control one step into the paper, the workaday grey chip a toolbar or a footer is full of, and the default. `filled` is the one action a view points at; `outlined` its drawn twin; `tinted` a quiet accent chip; `plain` looks like text at rest but keeps the box, because its recipe washes on hover.

props.title: Tints
props.description: Hover any of these: the hover and press states come from the same recipe, so a danger button darkens the way a primary one does. Nothing below sets a colour — each row is one variant read against six ramps. `recessed` and `normal` are absent on purpose: they are the neutral controls, reading the theme's surface and ink roles rather than a ramp, so `tint` leaves them untouched.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Button keeps no per-size block at all: the `[data-size]` profile carries the height, the padding, the radius and the type face, and the stylesheet reads them once.

props.title: Content
props.description: An icon is a child rather than a prop, so it costs the component no API and takes the button's own colour through `currentColor`. A shortcut is the one trailing slot, set in the button's colour at a lowered opacity — a key cap inside a button would read as a second control. There is no `loading` prop either: work in flight is a spinner in the label and `disabled` on the button.

props.title: In a row
props.description: Where more than one button sits together, the row is an ActionBar so the gap comes from the control scale. The confirming action goes last and is the only filled one: two filled buttons side by side ask the reader to choose which is the default.

props.title: Callout
props.description: A tinted notice that sits in the flow of a pane, above the thing it is about. That is the line between this and a Toast: a toast reports something that already happened somewhere else, a callout qualifies what you are looking at. The token graph gives it two type roles — a title and a description — so it is built for both, and drops the title when a one-line notice is all that is needed.

props.title: Tints
props.description: A callout always wears the tinted treatment; anything louder would be a dialog, not a callout. So the ramp is the only colour axis, and it is the whole message: `danger` is a failure, `warning` a caveat, `info` a fact worth knowing.

props.title: Card
props.description: The filled or bordered box the panels in a layout are built from. It is a container rather than a control, so its padding is uniform and comes off the spacing scale instead of the control scale, and it stays out of the shared state machine — a panel that washed under the pointer would read as something you can press.

props.title: Variants
props.description: Only `tinted` reads the tint; the rest resolve against the neutral surface and border roles. `raised` is a panel on the canvas, `sunken` a well inside one, `outlined` a boundary with no fill of its own.

children: Padding, gap, and radius all come from the size.

props.title: Tints
props.description: The tinted variant across every ramp: a 50 fill under a 200 border. The other three ignore `tint` entirely, so setting it on them is harmless and does nothing.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Padding, the gap between children, and the radius step together. Each step is a spacing token and a radius token, not a control profile — a card holds content rather than sitting in a row of controls.

props.title: What goes in one
props.description: A card is a flex column with the gap already set, so a heading row, a body, and a footer need no spacing of their own — only the row that has to spread its children apart. `sunken` is the recessed variant, for a region that holds something rather than being something.

props.title: Divider
props.description: A one-pixel rule. It carries no component tokens of its own: a separator is entirely described by a border colour and the hairline step of the spacing scale, and inventing `divider-*` aliases for those would only add a layer to read through.

props.title: Tones
props.description: The two border roles. `muted` is the lighter of the pair, for a rule inside a filled surface where the default would cut too hard; `default` is what separates one region from another.

props.title: Vertical
props.description: Stretches to its flex parent, so a toolbar row sizes it without a height being passed in. That is the whole reason it is a div rather than an `<hr>`: a rule that has to be told how tall it is will be told wrong somewhere.

props.title: In a container
props.description: A card already sets the gap between its children, so a divider adds only the line — it does not need margins, and giving it any would double the space the card had decided on.

props.title: EmptyState
props.description: What a pane shows before it has content: one muted line and at most one action. The surrounding chrome already names the pane, so there is no heading, no explainer copy, and no illustration. It centres in whatever it is given, so it needs no height of its own.

props.title: With and without an action
props.description: The action row takes the control gap rather than the block gap, because it holds controls. One action is the norm; two is the most it should ever carry, and only when neither is obviously the way out.

props.title: No glossary terms match this filter
Wording
props.description: An empty pane and an empty result are different states and read differently: one says nothing has been added, the other says a filter matched nothing. Copy is the only thing carrying that difference, so it has to be exact.

props.title: No glossary terms match this filter
KeyCap
props.description: One key, drawn three ways. It reads the theme's ink and surface roles directly and takes no tint — a key looks like a key whatever is around it. A cap says what the key *is*; where the key can be changed, that is a ShortcutRecorder instead.

props.title: Variants
props.description: `hint` — the default — is bare faint text in the display cut: the `⌘F` beside an empty search field, the `⌥2` in a card's corner, an aside the eye may skip. `strong` is the same a step darker, for a hint that has to survive on a busy row. `key` alone draws the cap — a recessed, chip-cornered fill with no border, since a key is pressed *into* the surface rather than raised off it — and is what a settings page lists shortcuts in.

props.title: Sizes
props.description: Colours are shared across the three; only the type steps, and only at the top — `small` and `medium` set the same face, `large` goes one up. Pick the size from what the key sits beside: `small` next to body text, `medium` in a row of controls.

props.title: Chords
props.description: A chord is several caps composed by the caller, which keeps the separator the caller's decision: macOS sets its modifiers flush, a cross-platform app usually wants a `+` between them. A hint sets the whole chord in one cap — `⌘⇧K` is one glyph run, not three — and the cap sits on the text baseline it is set in, so a sentence naming a shortcut does not gain a line of leading.

props.title: SectionLabel
props.description: The micro-heading that organises a pane. Sentence case, no uppercasing and no added tracking — one size covers sidebars, rails, and pane headings, so tone is the only axis worth varying. `SidebarGroupLabel` and `PreferenceSection` both render one for you; this is what those are made of.

props.title: Tints
props.description: Untinted it takes the muted content colour, which is what a heading almost always wants. A tint moves it onto a ramp, for a heading that has to carry a state with it — a section reporting a failure, a group flagged for review.

props.title: Over a panel
props.description: It names what the numbers below it are. The card already sets the gap, so the label needs no margin — which is the reason it is a span rather than a heading element with a browser margin to undo.

props.title: StepList
props.description: A pipeline, one line per stage. The marker carries the status — a check when a stage is finished, the spinner while it runs, an empty ring before it starts — so the label never has to say it twice. Each is a different marker rather than a different colour of the same one, which is what lets the column be read at a glance and still work in monochrome. The list holds no state: the host passes each stage its status.

props.title: In flight
props.description: A finished step is success wherever the list is tinted: it is the one fixed meaning in the column, not a variation on the accent. The trailing detail — a count, a duration, a size — is pushed to the far edge and set back, so a column of them lines up without competing with the labels.

props.title: Finished
props.description: Every stage done, so nothing in the column is asking for attention. This is the state a list should be able to end in without changing shape — no summary row appearing, no markers moving.

props.title: Tints
props.description: The tint reaches the active step — its spinner and its label. A finished step stays on the success ramp whatever the list is tinted with, because “done” is a fixed meaning rather than an accent.
